findings.paper_title: CAB 08/09 - Barrow Transformation Fund accelerate Housing Delivery
findings.headline: Barrow Transformation Fund governance transitioning to MHCLG control from October 2026
findings.detail: Council acts as Accountable Body for the £200m BTF under MOU with MHCLG. June 2026 MOU extends this role only 'during the transition period to a new delivery model from 01 October 2026, which is being led by MHCLG.' Council is committing to major delivery obligations while operational control transfers.
findings.matters: Uncertainty over funding continuation and council's role creates delivery risk; council committing to significant expenditure while governance transfers to MHCLG; potential disruption to delivery if transition is difficult
findings.figures: £19.5m anticipated annual payments (£13.5m capital, £6m revenue); £0.5m per year retained by MHCLG
findings.quote: An MoU was agreed in June 2026 for the Council to continue in the Accountable Body role during the transition period to a new delivery model from 01 October 2026, which is being led by MHCLG.

findings.paper_title: CAB 08/09 - Barrow Transformation Fund accelerate Housing Delivery
findings.headline: Housing delivery identified as critical to Defence Nuclear Enterprise workforce growth
findings.detail: Paper states employment growth from Defence/BAE expansion is 'unprecedented for the area' and housing delivery at current capacity is insufficient. Council explicitly warns that 'housing and planning constraints could impede workforce growth and undermine Barrow's ability to support the successful delivery of the UK's Defence Nuclear Enterprise.'
findings.matters: Housing delivery failure would impact Defence strategy success and Barrow's economic transformation, creating significant tax base and revenue risk for the council
findings.figures: £200 million Barrow Transformation Fund; approximately 1,350 new homes planned; unprecedented scale of employment growth anticipated
findings.quote: The scale of investment, employment growth and increase is unprecedented for the area, creating an urgent need for housing delivery at a pace and scale beyond that which can be supported through existing Council resources.

findings.paper_title: CAB 08/09 - Barrow Transformation Fund accelerate Housing Delivery
findings.headline: Officers delegated authority to modify development partner contract without finalised terms
findings.detail: Cabinet grants Strategic Director authority to make 'contractual modifications as may be required (including additional agreements)' with developer Muse ECF/Morgan Sindall. Paper states 'the detail of those modifications is still being discussed between the Council and Developer' with specific terms in confidential appendices. This supersedes the contract approved 20 January 2026.
findings.matters: Officers delegated authority to commit additional funding before contract terms are finalised; scope and cost of modifications not publicly disclosed; creates risk of costs beyond stated financial envelope
findings.figures: Original pre-development budget £1,175,925.09; assignment of additional funding to development partner not specified
findings.quote: make such contractual modifications as may be required (including additional agreements) to meet the ambitions stated in the business case, and within the financial envelope set out within the business case

findings.paper_title: CAB 08/09 - Barrow Transformation Fund accelerate Housing Delivery
findings.headline: Housing programme creates permanent staffing costs with acknowledged escalation risks
findings.detail: Cabinet approves establishment of an Accelerated Housing Delivery Team and expansion of Housing Standards capacity, generating new permanent revenue commitments. The paper explicitly identifies revenue escalation risks but does not quantify the revenue element separately or specify mitigation beyond the overall optimism bias.
findings.matters: New recurring revenue commitments created with acknowledged cost escalation risks; could pressure future budgets if labour market conditions drive salary costs above allocation
findings.figures: Revenue element not separately specified from £16.66m total; 24% optimism bias included overall
findings.quote: Other financial risks include the potential for revenue cost escalation, salary market pressures, changes in enabling works estimates, exposure to adverse market shifts and unforeseen revenue costs.

findings.paper_title: CAB 08/09 - Barrow Transformation Fund accelerate Housing Delivery
findings.headline: Council approves £16.66 million capital allocation for housing delivery acceleration
findings.detail: Cabinet approves allocation of £16.66m from the Barrow Transformation Fund including £11.38m for Marina Village strategic housing development (approximately 1,350 homes), £2.56m to support Defence Nuclear Enterprise and BAE Systems workforce housing needs, and £2.71m for Housing Standards team expansion. The allocation includes 24% optimism bias.
findings.matters: Material capital commitment from external government fund; council's delivery success is critical to supporting Defence Nuclear Enterprise economic growth in Barrow
findings.figures: £16.66m total allocation; £11.38m Marina Village; £2.56m Defence/BAE; £2.71m Housing Standards; 24% optimism bias; approximately 1,350 new homes planned
findings.quote: Approve, in its role as accountable body, the allocation of £16.66m of funding from the Barrow Transformation Fund to accelerate Housing Delivery in line with the Business Case

findings.headline: Levelling Up Fund regeneration schemes (Heart of Kendal and Barrow Market & Public Realm) are heavily deferred from 2026/27 to 2027/28, with grant funding also reduced.
findings.detail: Heart of Kendal was originally budgeted at £1.616m for 2026/27 but after a £1.366m grant reduction is forecast to spend only £0.250m in 2026/27, with £12.774m pushed to the following year. Barrow Market & Public Realm was originally £5.008m but after a £2.008m grant reduction is forecast at £3.000m in 2026/27 with £9.008m in 2027/28. Both represent more than 70% of the intended 2026/27 spend being deferred.
findings.matters: Major regeneration schemes funded by competitive government grants are being deferred by a year, suggesting potential delivery challenges (planning delays, land assembly, procurement) or funding changes that could affect when the council realizes the economic benefits of these investments.
findings.figures: Heart of Kendal: budget reduced by £1.366m, spending deferred from £1.616m to £0.250m in current year; Barrow: budget reduced by £2.008m, spending deferred from £5.008m to £3.000m in current year

findings.headline: Disabled Facility Grants budget jumped from £2.506m to £3.320m in Q1 (32% increase) through internal budget reallocation and grant changes.
findings.detail: The DFG line shows a virement (internal reallocation) of £1.214m added to the budget, which was partially offset by a £0.400m reduction in external grant funding. This £0.814m net increase occurred after the original budget had been set, indicating either recognition of higher-than-expected demand for home adaptations or prioritization of this service line. The revised Q1 budget of £3.320m forecast matches the Q1 outturn, suggesting it is tracking to plan.
findings.matters: A significant budget increase for disabled adaptations in the first quarter could signal emerging or accelerating demand for support to adapt homes for disabled residents, which may indicate ongoing cost pressures in adult social care that the council should monitor and fund.
findings.figures: Budget increased from £2.506m to £3.320m; £1.214m virement reallocation; £0.400m grant reduction

findings.headline: £27.992m (21% of the original budget) has slipped from 2026/27 to future years, with largest delays in Thriving Places (£14.294m), Children's Services (£4.818m), and Resources (£4.780m).
findings.detail: The council's total capital programme was originally budgeted at £130.497m for 2026/27. After Q1 revisions and accounting for scheme slippage, the revised budget for 2026/27 is £113.994m, meaning nearly a quarter of planned spending is being pushed to future years. The largest slippages affect major infrastructure and maintenance schemes including the A595 Grizebeck stage 2 road project (£3.500m), property maintenance and improvements across multiple services, and housing and community projects.
findings.matters: Material slippage across a fifth of the capital programme suggests systematic delays in delivering planned infrastructure, maintenance, and community projects, which could affect economic impact and the council's ability to execute its medium-term capital ambitions.
findings.figures: £27.992m slippage out of £130.497m original budget; Thriving Places £14.294m slippage, Resources £4.780m, Children's Services £4.818m
findings.quote: Total Council Capital Programme Schemes 130.497 0.000 10.862 0.574 0.053 (27.992) 113.994

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for CAB 08/09 - 2026/27 Quarter 1 Strategic Risk Report
findings.headline: Two new high-severity strategic risks added in Q1: cyber incident and data protection incident
findings.detail: The council has added two new risks to its strategic register in Q1 2026/27: 'Impact of a significant Cyber incident' and 'Impact of a Data Protection incident', both rated at score 20 (high-risk red category). These were not on the Q4 register, suggesting new vulnerability assessment or incident that prompted escalation.
findings.matters: New cyber and data protection risks escalating to strategic level may indicate recent incidents, vulnerability findings, or compliance failures. Cyber incidents can directly disrupt financial systems and council operations, with uninsured cost consequences.
findings.figures: 2 new risks added in Q1; both scored 20 (high-risk red category)
findings.quote: 2 new risks were added

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for CAB 08/09 - 2026/27 Quarter 1 Strategic Risk Report
findings.headline: Council cannot sustain prevention investment against rising health and social care demand from ageing population
findings.detail: The council identifies inability to sustain and increase prevention investment as a strategic risk rated 16 out of 25 (high-risk red category), driven by rising demand for health and social care services from an ageing population. Prevention funding is insufficient to meet demographic demand. No improvement from Q4.
findings.matters: Prevention underfunding in ageing populations typically leads to deferred costs manifesting as crisis demand on higher-cost adult social care and hospital discharge, creating unbudgeted cost pressures that become urgent and expensive.
findings.figures: Risk score 16 out of 25, no change from Q4 (Q4: 16, Q1: 16)
findings.quote: Inability to sustain & increase investment in Prevention to meet rising demand for Health & Social Care Services and the needs of an ageing population

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for CAB 08/09 - 2026/27 Quarter 1 Strategic Risk Report
findings.headline: Special Educational Needs system identified as financially unsustainable, risk score 15
findings.detail: The council rates 'Financially unsustainable Special Educational Needs system' at risk score 15 out of 25, in the high-risk red category. SEN is a statutory obligation where the council cannot currently fund provision at sustainable levels. Risk unchanged from Q4.
findings.matters: SEN is a statutory service with limited discretion to cut. Flagging it as unsustainable implies either significant overspend, rising needs, or structural funding inadequacy that will require intervention or exceptional reserve deployment.
findings.figures: Risk score 15 out of 25, no change from Q4 (Q4: 15, Q1: 15)
findings.quote: Financially unsustainable Special Educational Needs system

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for CAB 08/09 - 2026/27 Quarter 1 Strategic Risk Report
findings.headline: School system explicitly identified as financially unsustainable, rated risk score 20
findings.detail: The council rates 'Financially unsustainable school system' at risk score 20 out of 25, placing it in the high-risk red category. This is a specific service area where the council has concluded current funding is insufficient to sustain operations. No improvement from Q4.
findings.matters: Schools represent a significant council budget commitment. Classifying them as financially unsustainable suggests either rising costs, falling income, or structural underfunding that could force service reductions or exceptional financing.
findings.figures: Risk score 20 out of 25, no change from Q4 (Q4: 20, Q1: 20)
findings.quote: Financially unsustainable school system

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for CAB 08/09 - 2026/27 Quarter 1 Strategic Risk Report
findings.headline: Financial sustainability is the council's highest-rated strategic risk at maximum severity score 25
findings.detail: The council identifies 'Deliver a Financially Sustainable Authority' as its top strategic risk, rated at 25 out of 25 — the maximum possible risk score, placing it firmly in the red high-risk category. This risk received no improvement from Q4 2025/26 to Q1 2026/27, remaining static at 25.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand that this council has formally assessed its core financial viability as its single highest strategic priority, indicating structural financial challenges.
findings.figures: Risk score 25 out of 25 (maximum), no change from Q4 (Q4: 25, Q1: 25)
findings.quote: Deliver a Financially Sustainable Authority

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for CAB 08/09 - 2026/27 Quarter 1 Strategic Risk Report
findings.headline: Workforce engagement and retention challenges threaten delivery of transformation and savings during major retrenchment
findings.detail: The council faces sustained workforce capacity and engagement pressures during significant organisational transformation and budget reductions. The Director of HR reports risks from 'change fatigue arising from multiple concurrent programmes,' 'recruitment and retention challenges within key professional, technical and leadership roles,' and questions about whether staff understand the financial challenges and rationale for change.
findings.matters: Workforce instability during financial recovery could prevent delivery of transformation and savings programmes the council depends on to avoid financial failure.
findings.figures: Workforce risk scored 20/25; multiple concurrent transformation and restructuring programmes
findings.quote: If not carefully managed, these pressures could impact service continuity, delivery of statutory responsibilities, staff engagement and the Council's ability to successfully deliver its Transformation Programme and associated savings targets.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for CAB 08/09 - 2026/27 Quarter 1 Strategic Risk Report
findings.headline: High Needs Block (SEND) deficit will transfer to general budget from March 2028 when statutory override expires
findings.detail: The High Needs Block deficit is currently protected by a statutory override expiring March 31, 2028. Government's Stability Grant is expected to cover up to 90% of the cumulative deficit, but the remainder will fall to the council's general budget. This deferred liability will impact the budget during the council's period of maximum vulnerability.
findings.matters: Creates a known future financial shock of £millions that coincides with peak structural budget crisis, likely triggering inability to set legal budget.
findings.figures: Statutory override expires 31 March 2028; Stability Grant covers up to 90% of deficit
findings.quote: the remainder falls to the Council once the statutory override ends at the 31 March 2028

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for CAB 08/09 - 2026/27 Quarter 1 Strategic Risk Report
findings.headline: School balances forecast net deficit of £3.6m in 2026/27 with 28 schools predicting deficits
findings.detail: Schools are forecasted to have a net deficit of £3.624m in 2026/27, with 28 schools predicting individual deficits. While improved from 46 schools in deficit in March 2026, the Director of Education notes there are 'a small number of schools with significant deficits that continue to be a risk to the Council.'
findings.matters: School deficits directly deplete council reserves and compound financial sustainability pressures at a time when reserves are already at critical levels.
findings.figures: £3.624m net deficit forecast for 2026/27; 28 schools in deficit
findings.quote: The forecast net deficit is now £3.624m, this is an improvement of £1.196m compared to the October Budget submissions.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for CAB 08/09 - 2026/27 Quarter 1 Strategic Risk Report
findings.headline: Transformation programme critical to financial recovery faces significant workforce capacity and delivery risks
findings.detail: The council's financial sustainability depends on a transformation programme to deliver required savings. However, the transformation portfolio faces material workforce capacity constraints (scored 16 on the risk register), communications and technology risks, and is still in 'mobilisation and governance strengthening phase.' Non-delivery would result in savings shortfalls and a 'widening budget gap.'
findings.matters: Failure of the transformation programme means the £31m+ in identified but currently unfunded savings cannot be delivered, triggering financial failure.
findings.figures: Workforce capacity risk scored 16 across transformation programmes; £15m+ in savings dependent on delivery
findings.quote: Financial impact: non-delivery of savings, increasing upfront investment and a widening budget gap.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for CAB 08/09 - 2026/27 Quarter 1 Strategic Risk Report
findings.headline: Reserves insufficient to support budget beyond 2026/27; £31m+ in savings required for future years that cannot be funded
findings.detail: The council's reserves are not sufficient to support the budget beyond 2026/27. An additional £31m in savings must be identified for 2027/28, with a further £20m required for 2028/29. The Director of Finance states that 'earmarked reserves may support a moderate overspend in 2026/27 and then fall to absolute minimum levels' and that there is a 'significant risk that the 2026/27 budget will not remain balanced.'
findings.matters: Inability to fund identified future deficits from reserves indicates a structural budget crisis with no financial buffer, raising imminent risk of Section 114 notice.
findings.figures: £31m additional savings needed 2027/28; £20m additional savings needed 2028/29; reserves falling to minimum levels
findings.quote: The Council's reserves are not sufficient to support the budget beyond 2026/27, or to support the pacing of savings.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for CAB 08/09 - 2026/27 Quarter 1 Strategic Risk Report
findings.headline: Council faced £5.2m overspend in 2025/26 with £30.8m in savings needed just to balance 2026/27
findings.detail: The council's provisional outturn for 2025/26 showed an overspend of £5.220m. To achieve a balanced budget for 2026/27, the council must deliver £30.847m in savings. This aggressive target follows a Fair Funding Review that significantly reduced core government funding.
findings.matters: A £5.2m overspend in the previous year combined with the need for nearly £31m in savings indicates a council in acute financial distress with limited capacity for error in execution.
findings.figures: £5.220m overspend in 2025/26; £30.847m savings target for 2026/27
findings.quote: The provisional outturn for 2025/26 was an overspend of £5.220m. The main areas of recurring pressure were included in the 2026/27 Medium Term Financial Plan.

findings.headline: Drug and alcohol services in business continuity in Barrow due to funding challenges
findings.detail: The council is preparing to recommission drug and alcohol services before the current contract ends in Q2. The existing service in Barrow is currently in business continuity mode due to staff shortages linked to funding challenges and local workforce supply issues.
findings.matters: A critical public health service is operating in reduced capacity due to funding constraints, signalling a localised budget pressure within the council
findings.figures: Barrow area
findings.quote: The existing service is in business continuity at present in the Barrow area due to staff shortages, linked to funding challenges and local workforce supply.

findings.headline: SEND Reform Plan could write off 90% of High Needs Block deficit, decision expected September 2026
findings.detail: The council submitted a co-produced SEND Reform Plan to the Department for Education; a decision is expected in September 2026. If approved, 90% of the High Needs Block deficit will be written off through the High Needs Stability Grant. Early feedback from the DfE and financial advisers has been positive, with only minor amendments required.
findings.matters: A contingent 90% relief of the High Needs Block deficit is material to the council's financial position and will be determined within one month of this report
findings.quote: Approval would result in 90% of the High Needs Block deficit being written off through the High Needs Stability Grant. Early feedback from the DfE and financial advisers was positive, with only minor amendments required.

findings.headline: Workforce capacity constraints amid increasing service demand
findings.detail: Ensuring 'workforce capacity and capability to manage the demand and workload pressures' is identified as a high-scoring strategic risk. This reflects pressure to meet rising demand for adult and children's services while staffing.
findings.matters: Workforce gaps constrain the council's ability to deliver services and savings, and may indicate emerging cost pressures from agency/overtime spending
findings.figures: None specified
findings.quote: Ensuring we have the workforce capacity and capability to manage the demand and workload pressures.

findings.headline: Special educational needs and school systems identified as financially unsustainable
findings.detail: The council is 'trying to work within a financially unsustainable Special Educational Needs and Disabilities System and an unsustainable School System'. This is listed among the high-scoring strategic risks in the 2026/27 register.
findings.matters: SEND deficits are a known pressure on council budgets; identifying the system as unsustainable signals the council faces a structural budget challenge without additional funding
findings.figures: None specified
findings.quote: Trying to work within a financially unsustainable Special Educational Needs and Disabilities System and an unsustainable School System.

findings.headline: Care sector buildings at risk of unplanned closure due to end-of-life condition
findings.detail: Council care buildings are being maintained safely but there is 'concern over the potential impact of the disruptive closure of a building at no-notice, due to buildings coming to end of life and no longer being fit for purpose'. This emerging risk remains under consideration.
findings.matters: Unplanned care facility closure disrupts service delivery to vulnerable residents and could force emergency expenditure on alternative accommodation or outsourced provision
findings.figures: None specified
findings.quote: Council Buildings within the Care Sector are being maintained in a safe condition however, there is concern over the potential impact of the disruptive closure of a building at no-notice, due to buildings coming to end of life and no longer being fit for purpose.

findings.headline: Aging council buildings and highways requiring rationalisation and investment planning
findings.detail: A portfolio-wide condition survey of council buildings, highways, car parks and bridges is underway during 2026/27 to assess obsolescence. Assets with higher risk of 'physical, functional and economic obsolescence' are being identified. Each asset is RAG rated to enable decisions on 'asset rationalisation and investment planning'.
findings.matters: Aging assets may require unplanned capital investment or force service consolidation, affecting both capex requirements and operational sustainability
findings.figures: Portfolio-wide survey; specific asset counts not stated
findings.quote: With an ageing infrastructure, the Council continues to identify those assets with a higher risk of physical, functional and economic obsolescence. The risk of obsolescence has been identified across the portfolio of Council assets including office buildings, council-maintained schools, care sector buildings, car parks and bridges.

findings.headline: Financial pressure building with need for continuing savings action
findings.detail: The council faces 'severe financial strain' driven by rising service demand against cut funding. During 2025/26 financial pressure built, and the council now needs 'continuing management action to review known service pressures, future demand and to identify savings from service efficiencies and the Priority Programmes'.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council has identified credible savings and can execute them against service demand pressures
findings.figures: None specified in this report
findings.quote: Local Authorities continue to face severe financial strain, driven by the rising demand for essential services while funding for universal services are being cut. The same is true for Westmorland and Furness and during 2025/26 we have seen the level of financial pressure build, and in response there is a continuing need for management action to review known service pressures, future demand and to identify savings from service efficiencies and the Priority Programmes.

findings.headline: Multiple Levelling Up Fund and Town Deal schemes are being reprofiled away from 2026/27
findings.detail: Significant externally-funded regeneration schemes show deferrals: Levelling Up Fund schemes including Barrow Market & Public Realm (£2.008m), Heart of Kendal (£1.366m), and Eden Enterprise Hub (£0.658m) are all being pushed into later years. Town Deal schemes are similarly affected. High Needs Provision (£4.818m) reprof also suggests pressure on schools investment.
findings.matters: Deferrals of competitive external funding schemes may signal resource or delivery constraints; repeated reprofs could risk loss of grant conditions or timebound commitments that regeneration funding typically carries
findings.figures: LUF Barrow Market (2.008m), LUF Heart of Kendal (1.366m), LUF Eden Hub (0.658m), High Needs (4.818m)
findings.quote: Levelling Up Fund - Barrow Market & Public Realm (2.008) 2.008 0.000

findings.headline: £27.992m of capital spending is being deferred from 2026/27 to later years
findings.detail: The Q1 reprofs section shows the council moving approximately 25% of previously approved directly-delivered capital spending out of 2026/27, with major deferrals including High Needs Provision (£4.818m), A595 Grizebeck Stage 2 (£3.5m), Corporate Property maintenance (£2m), and LEVI Infrastructure (£1.793m). This significantly reduces 2026/27's capital investment from the February 2026 baseline.
findings.matters: Material annual reprofiling may indicate cost pressures, delivery constraints, or resource allocation changes that affect the council's ability to execute its capital strategy and maintain investment momentum in key services
findings.figures: Total Re-Profiles Quarter 1 2026/27: (27.992) moving to future years; Directly Delivered Schemes at Quarter 1 2026/27: 113.994m (2026/27 column); represents 24.5% reduction from previously approved spend

findings.headline: Total savings plan is £5.685 million (16%) short by Q1
findings.detail: The council is forecasting total savings of £30.348m against a plan of £36.033m across four categories. The variance is spread across adult services (£2.925m), workforce (£1.947m), LGPS pension scheme (£670k), and leisure/cultural services (£111k), with multiple items marked HIGH or MEDIUM RISK.
findings.matters: A 16% savings shortfall by Q1 (one-third through the year) is material and suggests the budget plan may not be achievable. If not recovered, the council could face a deficit requiring emergency action or reserve drawdown, affecting borrowing sustainability.
findings.figures: Total plan: £36,033,000 (Services £11.467m + Cross-cutting £8.642m + Other £10.738m + Existing MTFP £5.186m); Forecast £30,348,000; Variance £5,685,000
findings.quote: Forecast saving will be lower than budgeted

findings.headline: Workforce savings target is 38% short at mid-year
findings.detail: The cross-cutting Workforce Savings scheme is forecasting £3.113m against a £5.06m target—a shortfall of £1.947m. Marked MEDIUM RISK, the comment indicates 'Forecast saving will be lower than budgeted', suggesting implementation is significantly behind or targets were unachievable.
findings.matters: Workforce savings typically reflect fixed headcount reductions. A 38% shortfall by Q1 suggests staffing targets are not being met, requiring the council to find equivalent savings elsewhere or face a deficit.
findings.quote: Forecast saving will be lower than budgeted

findings.headline: Adult services savings of £2.925 million are not being delivered
findings.detail: The Promoting Independence & Wellbeing diagnostic review saving of £2m is marked HIGH RISK with zero forecast recovery. The Care Services saving is also underperforming with a £925k shortfall. Together these represent a £2.925m variance on adult services MTFP savings carried forward from prior years.
findings.matters: Adult services is demand-led and cost-pressured (demographics, inflation). If structured savings are unachievable, this signals structural budget pressure requiring either new compensating savings, service reductions, or reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: Diagnostic Review: £2,000,000 planned, £0 forecast (£2m gap). Care Services: £1,387,000 planned, £462,000 forecast (£925k gap).
findings.quote: Saving will not be met

findings.headline: Adult services catering contract costs are £84,614 over the budgeted pressure
findings.detail: The council allocated £100,000 for catering contract increases but is forecasting £184,614 spend. The overspend reflects additional pressure on food costs beyond initial estimates.
findings.matters: Care services are demand-led and cost-sensitive; cost pressures here can cascade if inflation in food/service provision continues to exceed budgets.
findings.figures: Budget £100,000, Forecast £184,614, Variance £84,614
findings.quote: Adults Catering contract increases (£100,000) (£184,614) £84,614 Additional pressure of £84,614 on food costs

findings.headline: Pay award costs are running £492,000 higher than the funded budget
findings.detail: The council budgeted £1,643,000 for pay award inflation but is forecasting £2,135,000 by end of year. This 30% overspend on the pay award allocation suggests the actual settlement or staffing numbers exceeded budget planning.
findings.matters: Pay is typically the largest council cost and overspends here forecast into future years; a finance director needs to know whether this is a one-off settlement or a structural increase.
findings.figures: Budget £1,643,000, Forecast £2,135,000, Variance £492,000

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1: Detailed Directorate Revenue Budget Q1
findings.headline: Barrow Crematorium closure extended to 6 months, creating £0.455m budget pressure (worsened from 3.5-month forecast in Period 2)
findings.detail: The Thriving Communities directorate forecasts a £0.455m pressure from Barrow Crematorium due to a forecast 6-month closure; this has deteriorated from the Period 2 forecast of 3.5 months, indicating the closure duration has extended. An additional £0.088m staffing pressure relates to the closure.
findings.matters: Service closures create unplanned budget pressures and deteriorating forecasts (P2 to Q1) suggest either poor planning or emerging complications; closures in income-generating services directly reduce revenue
findings.figures: £0.455m closure pressure. £0.088m staffing pressure. Extended from 3.5 months (P2 forecast) to 6 months (Q1 forecast).
findings.quote: £0.455m pressure on Barrow Crematorium due to forecast 6-month closure (this was forecast as 3.5 months in P2). Further £0.088m is due to staffing pressures.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1: Detailed Directorate Revenue Budget Q1
findings.headline: Housing Benefit subsidy shortfall of £0.35m, with £0.3m reclassified as a 'risk' rather than forecast outturn
findings.detail: The council faces a £0.35m anticipated shortfall between budgeted housing benefit and the subsidy received. Notably, £0.3m of this has been reclassified from forecast outturn to a 'risk' category, suggesting uncertainty about whether this will crystallise or whether mitigation is unconfirmed.
findings.matters: Housing benefit subsidy is fixed-cost; it is not within the council's control and cannot be addressed by service savings. Reclassification to 'risk' signals the mitigation is either unclear or may not be secure.
findings.figures: £0.350m total pressure. £0.300m reclassified to risk status (uncertain outcome).
findings.quote: Anticipated shortfall of housing benefit subsidy against housing benefit; £0.300m of the pressure has been reclassified from the forecast outturn to a risk.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1: Detailed Directorate Revenue Budget Q1
findings.headline: £2m Adult Services savings plan (Diagnostic Review) is forecast to fail entirely; separate Care Services savings only 25% likely to achieve
findings.detail: The Promoting Independence & Wellbeing - Adults Diagnostic Review was budgeted to deliver £2m of savings but is now forecast not to achieve. Additionally, Care Services savings of £1.387m are only 25% forecast to be achieved, meaning a shortfall of approximately £1.04m against plan.
findings.matters: Failed or severely underachieving savings plans indicate either weak demand forecasting or implementation/delivery challenges; this leaves budgets exposed to pressures and raises questions about the reliability of future savings plans
findings.figures: £2.000m Diagnostic Review (0% achievement forecast). £1.387m Care Services savings with 25% achievement rate (£1.04m shortfall forecast).
findings.quote: Promoting Independence & Wellbeing - Adults Diagnostic Review of £2.000m forecast not to achieve. Only 25% of the £1.387m saving forecast to be achieved.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1: Detailed Directorate Revenue Budget Q1
findings.headline: Adult Services facing £2.2m overspend driven by care cost pressures: Home Care £2.7m and Nursing Care £1.2m
findings.detail: The Adult Services directorate is forecasting a £2.214m overspend (2.12% of budget). The primary drivers are externally provided care packages: Home Care costs are forecast £2.739m over budget, Nursing Care £1.187m over, and Extra Care Housing £0.189m over. These pressures are only partially offset by surpluses in Residential (£2.418m) and Direct Payments (£1.394m).
findings.matters: Adult social care is a demand-driven cost the council cannot easily control; sustained pressures in Home Care and Nursing Care signal ongoing demographic and cost pressures that may constrain future budgets and repayment capacity
findings.figures: £2.214m directorate overspend (2.12% of £104.5m budget). Home Care £2.739m pressure, Nursing Care £1.187m, Extra Care Housing £0.189m. Offsets: Residential (£2.418m) underspend, Direct Payments (£1.394m) underspend.
findings.quote: Forecast pressure on Home Care of £2.739m, Nursing Care of £1.187m and Extra Care Housing of £0.189m; offset by forecast surplus on Residential of (£2.418m), Direct Payments of (£1.394m)

findings.headline: Council investing £0.180m in 15 new special school places to shift from independent to maintained provision
findings.detail: The SEND Reform Plan adds 15 new places to maintained and academy special schools (390 baseline plus 15 new from September 2026), estimated at £0.180m additional cost, with the intention of offsetting savings against independent placements. The strategy assumes all new places will be occupied.
findings.matters: This is a capital-to-revenue transformation strategy to reduce long-term SEND costs, but depends on both new places filling and independent placement numbers falling as assumed; if either assumption breaks, the council has committed additional spend with no offsetting saving
findings.figures: 15 new places, £0.180m cost
findings.quote: A total of 390 funded places from September 2026 are included in the baseline forecast position, plus a further 15 new places and associated top-ups are forecast as part of the SEND Reform plan mitigations which are estimated at an additional cost of £0.180m in total and is offset by a saving against independent special school placements and mainstream top-ups.

findings.headline: New independent school placements cost 11% more than those ending (£65,751 vs £59,202)
findings.detail: Independent special schools: 31 existing placements end in August averaging £59,202, but 44 new placements forecast (26 by September + 18 estimated) at £65,751. Post-16 shows an even steeper escalation: ending placements at £49,869 versus new ones at £65,995 (32% higher).
findings.matters: As the council rotates placement stock, unit costs per pupil rise substantially. Unless offset by volumes falling, this represents unbudgeted cost inflation that will accumulate through the year
findings.figures: Independent day: £65,751 new vs £59,202 ending; Post-16: £65,995 new vs £49,869 ending
findings.quote: The average cost of independent special school placements that are forecast to end in August is £59,202. However, the average cost of new placements is forecast to be £65,751 as at 31 March 2027.

findings.headline: EHCP numbers grew by 97 children in Q1 alone, with per-pupil top-up costs rising sharply
findings.detail: The council has 2,834 children with EHCPs as of June 2026, up 97 from March 2026. Mainstream EHCP top-ups increased £158 per child (now £8,388) and specialist bases £472 per child (now £10,037). This represents 3.5% quarterly growth in numbers.
findings.matters: Rapid SEND demand growth with cost inflation is a structural budget pressure that will accumulate across the financial year and may require reserve drawdown if the trend continues
findings.figures: 2,834 EHCPs (up 97), £8,388 average mainstream top-up (+£158), £10,037 specialist top-up (+£472)
findings.quote: The growth in demand for EHCPs continues, with the number of CYP with an EHCP at June 2026 at 2,834.  This is an increase of 97 compared to March 2026. The average top-up paid to a W&F mainstream student at P2 is £8,388, an increase of £158 since March 2026.

findings.paper_title: CAB 08/09 - 2026/27 Quarter 1 Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring Report to 30 June 2026
findings.headline: Contingency budget of £2.000m assumed to be fully used by year-end
findings.detail: The report states the £2.000m contingency budget 'is assumed to be used in full by the 31 March 2027', indicating it is already earmarked for known pressures rather than held as flexible cover.
findings.matters: A contingency fully committed at Q1 means the council has no buffer for in-year shocks or further cost pressures; any additional overspends will require further reserves or savings discovery.
findings.figures: £2.000m contingency assumed fully used
findings.quote: The contingency budget of £2.000m is assumed to be used in full by the 31 March 2027.

findings.paper_title: CAB 08/09 - 2026/27 Quarter 1 Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring Report to 30 June 2026
findings.headline: Reserves contribution of £10.271m drawn down to fund 2026/27 expenditure
findings.detail: The Council is using £10.271m from earmarked reserves (excluding DSG) to fund service expenditure in 2026/27. This is built into the budget but represents a one-off use that cannot be repeated indefinitely; combined with the £19.475m DSG pressure (also a cash drain on reserves through statutory override), this is material reserve depletion.
findings.matters: Reserve drawdown is acceptable for time-limited pressures but becomes a structural problem if needed every year; with £10.271m general drawdown plus £19.475m DSG cash cost, total reserve impact is £29.746m.
findings.figures: £10.271m reserves contribution; £19.475m DSG cash impact
findings.quote: The revised 2026/27 budget includes a net contribution from reserves of £10.271m to fund specific service expenditure.

findings.paper_title: CAB 08/09 - 2026/27 Quarter 1 Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring Report to 30 June 2026
findings.headline: Barrow Crematorium six-month closure generating £0.455m budget pressure
findings.detail: The closure of Barrow Crematorium is forecast to generate a £0.455m pressure in 2026/27. This appears to be a planned closure but the report provides no detail on duration, reason or the impact on service users or alternative provision.
findings.matters: Service closures that create budget pressures indicate either deferred maintenance/capital issues or demand-led service losses; the pressure suggests the council is absorbing income loss rather than recovering it.
findings.figures: £0.455m budget pressure
findings.quote: The six-month closure of Barrow Crematorium is forecast to generate a budget pressure of £0.455m.

findings.paper_title: CAB 08/09 - 2026/27 Quarter 1 Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring Report to 30 June 2026
findings.headline: Grounds maintenance contract overspend of £0.662m with contract review underway
findings.detail: Thriving Places directorate is forecasting a grounds maintenance overspend of £0.662m. The report confirms a contract review is underway 'to bring this back into line with budget as soon as possible' but provides no timeline or confidence level.
findings.matters: A material contract overspend in the early year suggests either contract terms that do not reflect current costs or service delivery volume challenges; the lack of detail on the review outcome indicates uncertainty on recovery.
findings.figures: £0.662m overspend forecast
findings.quote: The grounds maintenance contract is forecast to overspend by £0.662m; a contract review is underway to bring this back into line with budget as soon as possible.

findings.paper_title: CAB 08/09 - 2026/27 Quarter 1 Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring Report to 30 June 2026
findings.headline: Waste disposal contract overspend of £0.642m due to tonnage, landfill and SRF cost movements
findings.detail: The waste disposal contract hosted by Cumberland is forecasting a £0.642m deficit driven by updated assumptions on tonnage, landfill projections, inflationary uplifts on electricity and operational elements, SRF gainshare adjustments, and FAR movements. The report notes this reflects 'updated assumptions' but does not indicate whether this was unanticipated.
findings.matters: A £0.642m waste contract overspend indicates either forecasting/contract management issues or exposure to market volatility in energy and waste commodity costs; if this reflects uncontrollable external factors, it may recur.
findings.figures: £0.642m forecast deficit; waste is a major shared service
findings.quote: The waste disposal contract (hosted by Cumberland) is forecasting a deficit of £0.642m. This reflects updated assumptions across tonnage, landfill, electricity and SRF gainshare for the year

findings.paper_title: CAB 08/09 - 2026/27 Quarter 1 Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring Report to 30 June 2026
findings.headline: DSG High Needs Block cumulative deficit forecast at £52.509m by March 2027
findings.detail: The in-year pressure is £19.475m, bringing the cumulative deficit from £33.034m (carried forward from 2025/26) to £52.509m. Although covered by statutory override until March 2028, the council is providing the cash resources. Government has pledged to cover 90% of the historic deficit if a Local SEND Reform Plan is approved, but formal confirmation is still awaited.
findings.matters: DSG deficits, even with statutory override, represent a cash outflow and constraint on general reserves; dependency on government confirmation of support creates planning uncertainty.
findings.figures: £52.509m cumulative deficit forecast; £19.475m in-year pressure; £33.034m carried forward
findings.quote: A significant risk to the Council is the materiality of the High Needs DSG deficit estimated for 2026/27. Current forecasts estimate the deficit at £52.509m by 31 March 2027.

findings.paper_title: CAB 08/09 - 2026/27 Quarter 1 Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring Report to 30 June 2026
findings.headline: Cross-cutting workforce savings shortfall of £1.979m from salary sacrifice and redundancy schemes
findings.detail: Forecast workforce savings are £6.663m against a plan of £8.642m. The shortfall comes from a salary sacrifice scheme that has been replaced, part-year impact of voluntary redundancy, and the proposed mandatory Christmas closure. The report states 'alternative options and offers are being actively worked on' but provides no revised forecast.
findings.matters: If workforce savings do not recover in Q2/Q3, this represents a recurring structural gap that will require either service reductions or further reserves drawdown.
findings.figures: £1.979m variance; £8.642m planned workforce savings; £6.663m forecast
findings.quote: This variance covers a shortfall in current savings from a salary sacrifice scheme that has since been replaced by an alternative but similar saving, the part-year savings from the voluntary redundancy scheme and the proposed mandatory Christmas closure.

findings.paper_title: CAB 08/09 - 2026/27 Quarter 1 Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring Report to 30 June 2026
findings.headline: Adult Services undelivered savings of £2.924m representing half the directorate overspend
findings.detail: Adult Services is forecasting a £2.214m deficit, of which £2.924m comes from savings plans that have not materialised. The report notes these are being monitored but does not confirm recovery. These are recurring budget gaps that carry forward to future years.
findings.matters: Undelivered savings, especially of this magnitude in a large directorate, indicate either over-optimistic savings planning or delivery capability issues; recurring savings that slip become structural deficits in future years.
findings.figures: £2.924m undelivered; Adult Services total overspend £2.214m
findings.quote: Undelivered savings plans contribute £2.924m of the deficit at Q1.

findings.paper_title: CAB 08/09 - 2026/27 Quarter 1 Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring Report to 30 June 2026
findings.headline: Revenue budget forecast overspend of £5.879m against approved budget of £301.124m
findings.detail: The Council is forecasting net expenditure of £307.003m compared to the approved net budget of £301.124m. Management actions are underway to mitigate this position through focused CMT meetings and alternative savings strategies, but the report states 'risk remains' and these mitigations need to offset the deficit.
findings.matters: A material in-year overspend indicates either budget planning issues or cost control challenges; lenders need confidence that either the mitigations will work or that reserves can absorb it without threatening future viability.
findings.figures: £5.879m overspend; £301.124m approved budget; £307.003m forecast outturn
findings.quote: The forecast net expenditure position as at 30 June 2026 (Q1) is £307.003m, compared to the net budget of £301.124m. This is a forecast overspend of £5.879m.

findings.headline: Large accountable-body capital programmes (externally delivered schemes) adding £49.451m outturn
findings.detail: In addition to direct delivery, the council managed £49.451m of accountable-body schemes (projects delivered through external bodies like Combined Authorities or regional funds) that accelerated and reprofiled significantly: £3.935m accelerated from 2025/26, then £2.330m reprofiled out. The volatility suggests external partners' delivery constraints affect programme timing.
findings.matters: Reliance on external delivery creates exposure to third-party project delays and funding conditions outside direct council control.
findings.figures: Accountable Body Schemes Outturn 2025/26: £49.451m (vs approved £23.982m for direct delivery component). Accelerated £3.935m, then net virements out £2.330m.

findings.headline: £65.139m in additional capital investments added mid-year in February 2026
findings.detail: February 2026 Council meeting approved substantial additional capital investments totalling £65.139m, split across the multi-year programme. This followed approved schemes and came with offsetting project changes of (£4.426m). The scale suggests either a material reappraisal of capital priorities or new funding opportunity identified mid-year.
findings.matters: Mid-year addition of this scale indicates either unbudgeted capital needs or a change in funding availability that altered the council's capital strategy within the fiscal year.
findings.figures: Additional Investments February 2026 Council: £65.139m (appears to fund Direct Delivery Schemes totalling £530.099m across all years)
findings.quote: Additional Investments February 2026 Council 65.139 65.139

findings.headline: £10.053m of capital schemes slipped from 2025/26 into future years
findings.detail: Multiple capital projects deferred: A595 Grizebeck Stage 2 (£1.239m), Carriageway Future Programme (£1.116m), Bridges and Structures (£0.546m), and eleven smaller schemes. No single project failed catastrophically, but the pattern across diverse infrastructure (roads, flood resilience, property maintenance, disabled facility grants) suggests systemic delivery constraints.
findings.matters: Slippage reduces outturn against budget and can signal project management challenges, funding delays, or delivery constraints that affect the council's ability to execute its capital strategy.
findings.figures: Total Slippage Outturn 2025/26: (10.053m), slipped to 2026/27. Individual items range from £0.263m to £1.383m.

findings.paper_title: WFC 30/07 Capital Programme Update & Treasury Management 2025/26 Outturn Report
findings.headline: Treasury Management underspend of £6.300m is driven by £3.291m one-off saving from temporarily elevated interest rates on cash holdings.
findings.detail: The council achieved a £6.300m underspend in Treasury Management, of which £3.291m is explicitly identified as a one-off saving arising from high interest rates on the council's short-term cash balances. This benefit depends on interest rates remaining relatively high and is therefore temporary.
findings.matters: One-off treasury gains mask the underlying financial position; if interest rates fall, the council will face a corresponding loss of income that was offsetting other budget pressures.
findings.figures: Treasury Management underspend: £6.300m; One-off interest saving: £3.291m (2025/26 only)
findings.quote: This budget included a one-off saving of £3.291m in 2025/26 only, arising from the increased interest received on the Council's short-term cash balances, achievable as interest rates have remained relatively high.

findings.paper_title: WFC 30/07 Capital Programme Update & Treasury Management 2025/26 Outturn Report
findings.headline: Capital programme shows £10.053m total slippage, with £4.014m of infrastructure projects delayed from 2025/26 into 2026/27.
findings.detail: Five infrastructure projects slipped from 2025/26 to 2026/27: A595 Grizebeck Stage 2 (£1.239m), Carriageway Future Programme (£1.116m), Barrow Emergency Act Travel (£0.595m), Bridges & Structures (£0.546m), and Carriageway PSD Treatments (£0.518m). These delays affect roads and bridges, core infrastructure assets.
findings.matters: Slippage indicates the council is not delivering its capital plans to schedule and raises questions about project management capacity and whether service resilience improvements will be delayed.
findings.figures: Total slippage £4.014m requiring Council approval; A595 Grizebeck: (£1.239m), Carriageway Programme: (£1.116m), Barrow Emergency Act: (£0.595m), Bridges & Structures: (£0.546m), Carriageway PSD: (£0.518m)
findings.quote: Slippage of £2.669m was approved by Cabinet, and slippage of £4.014m requires approval by Council (see Table 5).

findings.paper_title: WFC 30/07 Capital Programme Update & Treasury Management 2025/26 Outturn Report
findings.headline: Council is deliberately avoiding new borrowing, choosing instead to offset approved borrowing against short-term cash reserves.
findings.detail: The council holds approved borrowing capacity but has implemented a strategy to avoid taking new loans, instead using short-term cash reserves to offset what would otherwise require borrowing. The council holds £74.6m in temporary investments earning 4.07% average interest and £173.6m in existing debt at 3.7% average interest rate.
findings.matters: This strategy depends on maintaining adequate cash balances and is exposed to interest rate movements; lenders need to understand the sustainability of avoiding new borrowing and whether the council's liquidity is sufficient for its capital plans.
findings.figures: Debt portfolio: £173.6m at 3.7% average interest; Temporary investments: £74.6m at 4.07%; no new external borrowing in the year
findings.quote: No new external borrowing has been undertaken in the year, with the Council implementing its strategy to offset previously approved borrowing with short-term cash reserves rather than incurring borrowing costs on new loans.

findings.headline: External auditors issued a disclaimed opinion on the 2024/25 Statement of Accounts
findings.detail: The Audit Committee approved the 2024/25 Statement of Accounts and Annual Governance Statement in February 2026 despite Grant Thornton (the appointed external auditors) issuing a disclaimed opinion rather than a standard audit opinion. The committee's approval was based on other sources of assurance built up across the year, not a normal audit sign-off.
findings.matters: A disclaimed opinion indicates the external auditors could not provide assurance on the financial statements in the normal way, suggesting significant uncertainties or limitations in audit scope. This raises questions about financial reporting reliability that directly affect lender confidence and require explanation.
findings.quote: In February 2026, the Audit Committee approved the 2024/25 Statement of Accounts and Annual Governance Statement. In view of the External Auditors' disclaimed opinion, the Audit Committee's consideration and approval was based on other sources of assurance built up across the year.

findings.headline: Priority delivery programmes underperforming with multiple 2025/26 objectives undelivered or scope altered
findings.detail: The council describes 2025/26 as 'a year for discovery, identification & decision making' with implementation to follow in 2026/27. At the end of Q4 2025/26, a number of priority programme objectives have not been delivered or had scope altered. While governance has tightened under the new CEO, the pattern of undelivered objectives creates execution risk around whether planned benefits and savings will materialise.
findings.matters: Transformation programmes are typically relied upon to generate future savings and efficiency gains. Slippage and scope changes suggest the council may not realise expected financial benefits on planned timescale.
findings.figures: Number of priority programme objectives not delivered or altered in scope; 2025/26 designated as discovery/decision phase with implementation in 2026/27
findings.quote: At the end of the 25/26 financial year there are a number of priority programme objectives that have not been delivered, or the scope has been altered to ensure altered outcomes were achieved.

findings.headline: Adult social care Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards referral volumes rising with persistent recruitment challenges (risk score 20)
findings.detail: DoLS referral volumes continue to rise. While the council is clearing more caseload, the risk of legal challenge remains high. The council has faced difficulty recruiting Best Interests Assessors (BIAs) and is now relying on agency resource to manage demand. This represents both rising service demand and growing reliance on external staffing.
findings.matters: Rising DoLS referrals represent both growing service demand and potential legal liability. Agency staffing indicates tight internal capacity and adds cost to service delivery.
findings.figures: Referral volumes still rising; reliance on agency BIA resource
findings.quote: Referral volumes are still rising, and while we are clearing more caseload, the risk of challenge remains high. It remains difficult to recruit Best Interests Assessors (BIA) but agency resource has now been agreed.

findings.headline: SEND system deficit reduced to score 15 but remains uncertain pending complex government reform plan submission
findings.detail: Risk score reduced from 20 to 15 following government recognition of the national systemic nature of SEND deficits and publication of the White Paper (Every Child Achieving and Thriving). However, there remains uncertainty as to what proportion of the cumulative SEND deficit the government will write-off; this depends on the council submitting a complex SEND Reform Plan in Q1 2026/27. The council has reduced spend on Independent School Places through its Better Value plan.
findings.matters: SEND has been a persistent unfunded pressure on councils nationally. While government reform is underway, the outcome for this council depends on plan submission success and government policy decisions outside its control.
findings.figures: Risk score reduced from 20 to 15; reduction in Independent School Places spend through Better Value plan
findings.quote: The publication of the White Paper (Every Child Achieving and Thriving), SEND Reform consultation and guidance on applications for a HNB Stability Grant has allowed for a reduction in the likelihood of the risk arising, but there remains uncertainty as to the proportion of the cumulative deficit which could be written-off.

findings.headline: Major workforce restructuring underway with identified risk of inability to maintain statutory service delivery
findings.detail: The council has completed a voluntary redundancy scheme and implemented Phase 1 of Senior Leadership restructure. Further phases and service-led restructures are in development. The risk register explicitly identifies that the pace and scale of change may result in change fatigue, reduced engagement and loss of key skills. The council flags that this could impact its ability to consistently deliver statutory services, maintain safe operations and deliver required transformation.
findings.matters: Large-scale restructuring creates execution risk and service quality risk. The council's own assessment that workforce changes could impair statutory service delivery is a direct indicator of capacity constraints.
findings.figures: Voluntary redundancy scheme completed; Phase 1 Senior Leadership restructure implemented; further phases in development
findings.quote: There remains a risk that the pace and scale of change may result in change fatigue, reduced engagement and the loss of key skills where not effectively managed. This could impact the Council's ability to consistently deliver statutory services, maintain safe operations and deliver transformation.

findings.headline: DSG (Dedicated Schools Grant) deficit growing with council liability for write-off uncertain and dependent on government policy
findings.detail: The DSG deficit is growing. While government reform changes (SEND Reform Plan, HNB Stability Grant) are in train for 2026/27 through 2028/29, there is explicit uncertainty as to what proportion of the cumulative DSG deficit will fall to the council. This depends on successful submission of a complex SEND Reform Plan in Q1 2026/27. The report notes over 30 schools currently hold cumulative DSG deficits.
findings.matters: The timing and scale of DSG deficit recovery is contingent on national government policy and the council's ability to submit a successful reform plan. This is a material contingent liability with timing risk.
findings.figures: DSG deficit growing; over 30 schools with cumulative DSG deficits; proportion council will bear depends on 2026/27 government decisions
findings.quote: The DSG deficit is growing and although there are changes in 2026/27 through to 2028/29, the balance at 31 March 2028 will, in some part, fall to the Council.

findings.headline: School system deficit of £4.820m as at 31 March 2026 with 46 schools in deficit, deteriorating mid-year
findings.detail: The draft outturn shows a total school deficit balance of £4.820m, an increase of £0.909m compared to Q3 (indicating mid-year deterioration). There are 46 schools in deficit. Finance review meetings have been held with 35 affected schools. The School Deficit Balance Policy has been strengthened and Finance notes of concern have been issued to schools.
findings.matters: School deficits represent unfunded liabilities that the council ultimately carries. The scale (£4.820m) and upward trajectory mid-year suggest the council underestimated school funding needs and now faces a growing commitment.
findings.figures: £4.820m school deficit at 31 March 2026; increase of £0.909m from Q3; 46 schools in deficit
findings.quote: Draft outturn is an overall school deficit balance £4.820m an increase of £0.909m compared to Q3. There are 46 schools in deficit as at 31 March 2026.

findings.headline: Financial sustainability at critical risk (score 25) with £6m Q3 overspend and structural deficits persisting into future years
findings.detail: The council forecast a £6m overspend to 31 March 2026 in Q3. The S151 Officer has introduced new controls including weekly Spend Control Board reviewing all requests of £30k and above plus recruitment. Despite proposing a balanced budget for 2026/27, this requires significant savings and large deficits remain to be addressed in future years. The Medium-Term Financial Plan and reserves position are explicitly identified as high risks to future sustainability.
findings.matters: Structural overspends and forward-year deficits indicate the council's recurrent spending exceeds sustainable revenue. A lender needs confidence that the council can operate within its means; dependence on one-off reserves or unproven savings is a lending risk.
findings.figures: £6m overspend forecast Q3 2026; 2026/27 budget requires significant savings; large deficits in future years
findings.quote: The Q3 budget forecast was c£6m overspend for 31 March 2026... Large deficits remain to be addressed in future years.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement growing from £281.6m (2026/27) to £336m (2030/31)
findings.detail: The council's underlying borrowing need is expanding across the forecast period, reflecting continued capital investment. The CFR will grow by 19% over five years, increasing the long-term debt burden.
findings.matters: A growing CFR indicates increasing reliance on long-term borrowing to fund capital assets, with implications for intergenerational equity and long-term affordability.
findings.figures: General Fund CFR rises from £269.315m to £326.996m; Total borrowing need rises from £281.623m to £336.038m

findings.headline: £15m loans maturing in 2026/27 requiring refinancing at potentially higher rates
findings.detail: Significant debt maturity in the coming year will need to be refinanced. The timing and rates at which this is refinanced will depend on market conditions and the council's borrowing decisions.
findings.matters: Maturing debt must be refinanced, and depending on interest rates at refinancing, this could increase the council's annual debt service costs significantly.
findings.figures: £15.0m of loans maturing during 2026/27
findings.quote: The Council has loans of £15.0m maturing during 2026/27 and this is expected to be replaced with new borrowing.

findings.headline: Council maintaining under-borrowed position by drawing down £102.3m cash balances instead of external borrowing
findings.detail: Rather than externalising borrowing, the council is running down temporary cash reserves to finance capital and revenue needs. This defers costs but limits financial resilience and flexibility when cash runs low or when interest rates make deferral uneconomic.
findings.matters: This strategy temporarily reduces debt costs but exposes the council to interest rate risk and constrains flexibility if cash balances deplete faster than forecast.
findings.figures: £102.3m of cash balances projected to be used in lieu of external borrowing as at 31 March 2026
findings.quote: It is projected that as at 31 March 2026 c. £102.3m of cash balances will be used in lieu of external borrowing.

findings.headline: Capital programme of £122.6m in 2026/27 with £25.4m financed by prudential borrowing
findings.detail: The council plans substantial capital expenditure, with nearly a quarter to be financed through new borrowing. This drives the underlying capital financing requirement and future debt servicing costs.
findings.matters: The scale of capital plans determines future borrowing needs and debt service obligations, which directly affects the council's financial capacity.
findings.figures: £122.637m total capital expenditure; £25.4m prudential borrowing in 2026/27
findings.quote: Estimates of proposed capital expenditure... Total 122.637 [£m]... Estimates of proposed capital expenditure funded by prudential borrowing... 25.400 [£m]

findings.headline: Financing costs rising to 6.78% of revenue by 2030/31, up from 4.02% in 2026/27
findings.detail: The ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream increases materially over the five-year forecast period. This reduces the council's financial flexibility and constrains the resources available for service delivery, as an increasing share of revenue must service borrowing.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand how much of the council's revenue is consumed by debt service, and this trajectory shows significant fiscal tightening ahead.
findings.quote: Ratio of Finance costs to Net Revenue Stream 4.02% 5.30% 6.08% 6.44% 6.78%

findings.headline: External audit flagged DSG (Dedicated Schools Grant) deficit as a key issue; capacity constraints also identified across multiple external assessments
findings.detail: Grant Thornton's 2024/25 audit highlighted a DSG deficit, governance improvements still needed, and capacity constraints. CQC assessed Adult Social Care as 'Requires Improvement' (score 62/100), citing service performance impacted by 'delays, provision and capacity constraints'. LGA Corporate Peer Review called for 'sharper focus, faster delivery and stronger organisational grip'.
findings.matters: A DSG deficit is a specific unfunded liability. Consistent feedback on capacity from three independent external assessors suggests genuine resource constraints affecting service delivery and financial stability.
findings.figures: CQC score 62/100 (requires improvement); DSG deficit not quantified
findings.quote: Grant Thornton (External Audit) – Annual Audit Report 2024/25 (February 2026) – concluded Council had strong foundations, stable finances, good governance arrangements and positive service performance in key areas. However, highlighted key issues in terms of DSG deficit, improving governance, capacity in some areas and performance management

findings.headline: Financial system complexity persists: consolidated from 5 legacy ledgers to 1, but feeder system interfaces still require simplification
findings.detail: By 31 March 2026, the council retired all legacy financial ledgers to a single ledger system. However, Internal Audit notes work is 'ongoing to simplify feeder system interfaces', indicating the underlying architecture remains complex and potentially fragile.
findings.matters: Complex feeder systems increase risk of data errors, delays in financial reporting, and operational disruption. Unfinished system work suggests the finance function is not yet optimised.
findings.figures: Consolidated from 5 to 1 financial ledger effective 1 April 2026
findings.quote: The move from five to one financial ledger will support greater internal control although work is ongoing to simplify feeder system interfaces.

findings.headline: High concentration of strategic risks: 10 of 16 risks rated as 'high' by Quarter 3, up from 8 of 17 in Quarter 1
findings.detail: The council's strategic risk register deteriorated through the year, with the proportion of high-rated risks increasing. Risk Appetite Statement and Risk Framework remain incomplete and are only now being finalised (due to CMT for July 2026). This suggests risk governance frameworks lag behind risk exposure.
findings.matters: 62% of strategic risks at high severity indicates the council is managing substantial operational challenges. A lender would need to understand which specific risks these are and whether management frameworks are adequate.
findings.figures: Q1: 8 high out of 17 total risks; Q3: 10 high out of 16 total risks
findings.quote: The 2025/26 Quarter 1 Strategic Risk Report and Risk Register for Westmorland and Furness Council contained 17 strategic risks identified as relevant to the operation of the Council, with 8 risks rated as high and 9 rated as medium. By Quarter 3 of 2025/26 there were 16 strategic risks identified as relevant to the operation of the Council, with 10 risks rated as high and 6 rated as medium.

findings.headline: 23% of completed risk-based audits received only partial assurance; one multi-year issue (Business Continuity) remains unresolved
findings.detail: Of 26 completed audits, 6 resulted in partial assurance ratings (23%), meaning weaknesses were identified that could place achievement of objectives at risk. A follow-up review of Business Continuity Planning remains at partial assurance despite previous audit, suggesting slow remediation pace.
findings.matters: Multiple partial assurance ratings indicate control deficiencies across operational areas. Slow progress on follow-ups suggests the council struggles to remediate audit findings in a timely way.
findings.figures: 6 out of 26 audits (23%) partial assurance; 20 out of 26 (77%) reasonable or substantial
findings.quote: Of the 26 risk based audits (excludes schools) completed, or at draft report stage, 20 received reasonable or substantial assurance (77%), whilst 6 resulted in partial assurance (23%).

findings.headline: Significant payments being made without purchase orders; external audit flagged this, remediation planned for 2026/27
findings.detail: External audit identified a material control weakness: many payments are processed without corresponding purchase orders. Management is developing a 'No PO No pay' policy but has not yet implemented it. Implementation will be considered as part of accounts payable work in 2026/27, meaning the control gap persists through at least March 2027.
findings.matters: Uncontrolled payments increase fraud and error risk. A lender would need confidence in payables controls; a multi-year gap before remediation is concerning.
findings.figures: Not quantified in report; described as 'significant number'
findings.quote: The issue of a significant number of payments being made without a corresponding purchase order was highlighted by external audit. Management are currently looking at this issues and plan to introduce a policy of 'No purchase order (PO) No pay'. The implementation of this will be considered as part of our work on accounts payable in 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: CAB 17/03 - 2025/26 Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring report to 31 December 2025
findings.headline: Earmarked reserves are being drawn down with £1.071m used in Q3 for immediate pressures
findings.detail: Q3 drew £1.071m from earmarked reserves: Enabler Services £0.673m for ICT programme, Resources £0.382m for Housing Benefit settlement, Thriving Places £0.016m for grant matching. Net projected reserves position at 31 March 2026 is (£34.586m) with gross reserves (£71.497m).
findings.matters: Ongoing drawdowns of earmarked reserves reduce financial flexibility and shock-absorption capacity, indicating the council is using reserves to manage operational pressures rather than fund strategic investments.
findings.figures: Q3 draws £1.071m (Enabler £0.673m, Resources £0.382m); net reserves forecast (£34.586m); gross reserves (£71.497m)
findings.quote: During Quarter 3 £1.071m of earmarked reserves have been drawn down for: Thriving Places £0.016m; to match grant expenditure; Enabler £0.673m; ICT programme project expenditures; Resources £0.382m; Housing Benefit Subsidy claim settlement

findings.paper_title: CAB 17/03 - 2025/26 Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring report to 31 December 2025
findings.headline: Treasury Management underspend of £5.564m is masking underlying operational pressures and depends on interest rates
findings.detail: The council is not undertaking new external borrowing in 2025/26, instead using short-term cash reserves to offset approved borrowing plans. This avoids £3.705m in borrowing costs. Higher-than-budgeted interest rates produce £2.286m additional income. Together this £5.564m underspend significantly masks the £11.349m directorate overspend.
findings.matters: The council's true operating position is worse than headline figures suggest. This financial relief is temporary and dependent on interest rate maintenance. If rates fall, the underlying £11.349m operational deficit will be exposed.
findings.figures: £5.564m Treasury Management underspend (£3.705m avoided borrowing, £2.286m additional interest); no new external borrowing undertaken
findings.quote: No new external borrowing has been undertaken in the first nine months of 2025/26, with the Council implementing its strategy to offset previously approved borrowing with short term cash reserves rather than incurring borrowing costs on new loans. This strategy has generated £3.705m savings in the year.

findings.paper_title: CAB 17/03 - 2025/26 Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring report to 31 December 2025
findings.headline: Adult and Children's Services forecast demand-driven overspends of £4.926m and £5.111m respectively
findings.detail: Adult Services forecasts £4.926m overspend with Residential & Nursing Care £4.327m, Home Care £3.001m, and Supported Living £1.150m pressures, reflecting continued high demand. Children's Services forecasts £5.111m overspend with Cared for Children demand £2.075m, SEND transport £1.835m (driven by 21 net new pupils in 2025/26), and Home to School transport £0.858m (higher than 2024/25 demand).
findings.matters: Growing statutory demand for social care and education services that the council cannot control represents a major structural budget pressure that will recur annually unless the council reduces placements or the government changes funding.
findings.figures: Adult Services: Residential/Nursing £4.327m, Home Care £3.001m, Supported Living £1.150m; Children's: Cared for Children £2.075m, SEND transport £1.835m, Home to School transport £0.858m
findings.quote: Demand fluctuates but remains high for Residential and Nursing Care, Home Care and Supported Living, with respective forecast variances of £4.327m, £3.001m and £1.150m.

findings.paper_title: CAB 17/03 - 2025/26 Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring report to 31 December 2025
findings.headline: Agency staffing costs are significant and persistent across Adult Services, Child Protection and Waste
findings.detail: Adult Services Older Adults forecasts £2.023m pressure driven by 'the use of costly agency staff to fill vacancies and cover sickness.' Child Protection has £0.691m pressure from 'continued reliance on agency workers to cover vacancies and maternity leave.' Waste Services has £0.913m agency cost pressure. This pattern indicates the council cannot recruit or retain permanent staff in front-line statutory services.
findings.matters: Persistent agency staffing is costly and indicates deeper recruitment and retention challenges that may affect service delivery quality and sustainability.
findings.figures: £2.023m Older Adults staffing pressures; £0.691m Child Protection agency; £0.913m Waste Services agency costs
findings.quote: In Older Adults, the predicted deficit of £2.023m is driven by staffing pressures, with the use of costly agency staff to fill vacancies and cover sickness.

findings.paper_title: CAB 17/03 - 2025/26 Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring report to 31 December 2025
findings.headline: Approved savings of £11.045m are delivering only £9.634m, with £1.411m undelivered
findings.detail: The council's transformation savings programme is underperforming. Adults Promoting Independence diagnostic (£1.000m) is undeliverable due to delays. Children's Home to School Transport saving (£0.100m) is not delivering as demand increases offset savings. Staff Turnover vacancy saving (£0.311m of £0.600m plan) is failing as vacancies are covered by agency staff rather than left unfilled.
findings.matters: Undelivered savings indicate the council's transformation programme is not progressing as planned. This adds to the year-end deficit and signals challenges in executing strategic change.
findings.figures: £1.411m total shortfall: Adults Promoting Independence £1.000m, Children's transport £0.100m, Staff Turnover £0.311m of £0.600m plan
findings.quote: Adults Promoting Independence – Diagnostic (£1.000m): undeliverable in 2025/26 due to delays commencing the initial diagnostic work. No alternatives have been proposed to mitigate this.

findings.paper_title: CAB 17/03 - 2025/26 Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring report to 31 December 2025
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit has grown to £34.775m, driven by rising SEN demand
findings.detail: The cumulative DSG deficit is forecast at £34.775m by March 2026 (up from £22.135m brought forward). The High Needs Block alone is £40.143m in deficit. The in-year pressure deteriorated by £0.891m from Q2 to £12.640m. Growth in EHCPs is the driver: 2,692 children as at 31 December 2025, representing 8.5% growth since March 2025. The council's EHCP rate exceeds national and statistical neighbour averages.
findings.matters: This represents a structural, recurring deficit that the statutory override currently separates from general reserves but which signals growing unfunded statutory demand that will require either government funding confirmation or future council funding solution.
findings.figures: £34.775m cumulative DSG deficit; High Needs £40.143m deficit; in-year pressure £12.640m (£0.891m worse than Q2); 2,692 EHCPs (+8.5% since March 2025)
findings.quote: The number of children and young people with an EHCP as at 31 December 2025 is 2,692; an increase of 8.5% since March 2025.

findings.paper_title: CAB 17/03 - 2025/26 Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring report to 31 December 2025
findings.headline: Revenue budget forecast to overspend by £5.839m despite management actions
findings.detail: The council's revised budget is £307.271m but forecast outturn is £313.110m.
